modelName: A hybrid co-op — where the value goes and where the money goes
modelNote:
A worker-and-consumer hybrid (multi-stakeholder / solidarity) cooperative, drawn as circuits that do not have the same shape. GREEN is value moving — labour in, goods out. AMBER is money moving the other way: Odum's counterflow. BLUE dashed is money that does not leave — member capital. PURPLE is governance. Turn the layers on in that order (Value, Money, Capital, Governance) and the argument builds itself.

The argument: the surplus split on the right-hand side is the one members argue about at the annual meeting, and it is the small one. The big split happens at the till and on the payroll, before any surplus exists — the price a consumer member pays and the wage a worker member is paid come out of the same revenue, are set by the same board, and each is the other's cost. That is the structural fact a single-class co-op never has to face, and it is why the two purple arrows leaving THE BOARD are the most important pair on the drawing.

Three asymmetries the drawing is built to expose. (1) A consumer's patronage refund is treated by the IRS as a rebate on a purchase and is generally not taxable to them; a worker's patronage dividend is income and is fully taxable. Same dollar, different value on arrival, so the two classes are not indifferent to which channel it takes. (2) Consumers patronise in dollars spent and workers in hours worked, so the classes are not measured in the same unit and no formula converts one to the other — the bylaws simply have to say. (3) Margin earned on non-member business cannot be paid out as patronage at all; it is taxed at corporate rates and what survives can only fall to the indivisible reserve. That is why who is and is not a member is a money question and not only a values question.

Sources: Margaret Lund, 'Solidarity as a Business Model: A Multi-Stakeholder Cooperatives Manual' (Cooperative Development Center, Kent State, 2011) — member classes, governance-seat allocation, and the surplus-distribution decision. Weaver Street Market, Carrboro NC — the worked worker+consumer hybrid: about 4,000 consumer owners and 60 worker owners, a board of seven with 2 consumer seats, 2 worker seats, 2 appointed for skills, plus the General Manager; consumer dividends on purchases, worker dividends on hours, and the different tax landing for each. Eroski (Mondragon) — worker members buy in by payroll deduction over three years, take up to 30% of the annual distribution in cash, and recover the internal capital account with interest on leaving. IRC Subchapter T — at least 20% of a patronage refund in cash, the balance as a qualified written notice of allocation; non-member margin to indivisible reserves on an after-corporate-tax basis. Canadian Worker Co-op Federation and the Quebec Cooperatives Act — the indivisible reserve, 10% to 100% of annual surplus, never divisible among members.

Drawn by Claude for Marc Pierson, Aug 23 2026. Counterflow notation after Odum. This is an actor-and-flow map, not a causal map — polarity is deliberately unset and it should not be read as a CLD. Promoted to a declared value network 2026-08-31 (graphAttrs.method=vna). It was already one: the four legend rows carry Allee’s tangible/intangible split under other names, and the value/money pair is Odum counterflow. EVIDENCE: every arrow is marked “asserted” — this is a generic structural model of a hybrid co-op, not a measured one. Upgrade an arrow to “observed” only when a bylaw, contract or ledger backs it. IAD LEVEL: collective-choice (asserted 2026-08-31, open to correction at the Ostrom Workshop). Spans. Goods, labour and price at the till are operational, but the file exists to argue the board decision — sets PRICE and WAGE, sets the split. That is collective choice determining the payoff rules of the exchange below it.

legendEntries.label: A member class — owns it, patronises it its own way
The co-op itself — where the deciding is done
Where money sits — a till, a pot, a reserve
money that stays in — member capital
governs — one member one vote, inside a class

nodes.label: The split members argue about is on the right. The split that decides everything is at the till and on the payroll — before there is any surplus to argue about.
nodes.note: In a single-class co-op the price (or the wage) is a cost paid to outsiders and the members' interest in it runs all one way. In a hybrid, both sides of that trade are owners. The board that sets the consumer price and the board that sets the worker wage is the same board, spending the same revenue.

nodes.label: Consumers patronise in dollars spent. Workers patronise in hours worked. No formula converts one into the other — the bylaws have to just say.
nodes.note: This is the sentence that makes a multi-stakeholder co-op harder to write than a single-class one. Lund is explicit that participation and patronage happen differently for different classes, and that the surplus split need not follow the governance split at all.

props.basis: Lund, Solidarity as a Business Model (2011), 'Distribution of Surplus'

nodes.label: SUPPLIERS
nodes.note: Sell to the co-op, own none of it. In a food co-op this is where a third membership class often gets added — farmer-producers — turning the hybrid into a three-class solidarity co-op and giving the cost-of-goods arrow a patronage return of its own.

nodes.label: CONSUMER MEMBERS
nodes.note: Patronise by buying. Their stake is access and price. Equity contribution is generally low — one share, bought once, which buys the vote rather than the return. At Weaver Street Market there are roughly 4,000 of them against 60 worker owners, which is exactly why board seats are allocated by class and not by headcount.

props.name: Consumer members
props._basis: Lund Table 1; Weaver Street Market ownership figures

nodes.label: WORKER MEMBERS
nodes.note: Patronise by working. Their stake is livelihood — Lund's table rates it HIGH, where the consumer's is low-to-high depending on whether another shop exists. A worker member cannot shop elsewhere for a job as easily as a consumer member can shop elsewhere for groceries, and the governance design has to answer that asymmetry rather than pretend it away.

props.name: Worker members
props._basis: Lund Table 1, Variations in Potential Multi-stakeholder Membership Classes

nodes.label: NON-MEMBER SHOPPERS
nodes.note: Pay the same price and get the same goods. What they do not generate is patronage-allocable margin. Every hybrid has to decide how hard to push these people into membership, and NON-MEMBER MARGIN is the money reason to.

nodes.label: THE BOARD
nodes.note: Seats are allocated BY CLASS, and the allocation is not proportional to headcount. Weaver Street Market: seven seats — 2 elected by consumer owners, 2 by worker owners, 2 appointed by the board for particular skills, plus the General Manager. Quebec caps supporter members at one third of seats however many of them there are. Watch the two purple arrows leaving this node: they are the same decision, and only one of them is ever put to the membership.

props.name: Board of directors
props._basis: Weaver Street Market board composition; Lund on the Quebec supporter-seat cap

nodes.label: THE CO-OP
nodes.note: The operating enterprise. Notice what runs through here and what does not: ALL the value passes through this node and NONE of the money does — the money circuit runs through the till instead. That is the counterflow drawn honestly. The two circuits genuinely have different shapes, which is the test for whether drawing them as two lines earns its keep.

nodes.label: LENDER & LANDLORD
nodes.note: The claim that is paid whatever kind of year it was, to people who own no part of the enterprise. The more of the business financed from member equity and the reserve, the smaller this arrow — which is the whole practical case for retaining patronage rather than paying it all out in cash.

nodes.label: THE TILL
nodes.note: Every dollar the co-op receives, from members and non-members alike, at the same price. Four claims come out of it before anything is called surplus: goods, wages, occupancy and interest. Three of those four go to outsiders. One goes to owners.

nodes.label: MEMBER EQUITY
nodes.note: One internal capital account per member, in both classes. Filled from three directions: the share bought at joining, the payroll deduction, and — much the largest over time — the retained portion of each year's patronage. Eroski's worker members pay in by deduction over three years, take up to 30% of the annual distribution in cash, and recover the balance with interest when they leave. Note what this makes it: a liability with a long fuse. A co-op facing a retirement bulge or a shrinking town has a redemption problem that no income statement shows, which is why Lund puts transfer and dissolution rules among the founding board's most important decisions.

props.name: Member equity accounts
props._basis: Eroski / Mondragon internal capital accounts; IRC Subchapter T written notices of allocation

nodes.label: THE RESERVE
nodes.note: Indivisible. Never allocated to a member, never paid out, and it does not decrease. Quebec mandates it — 10% to 100% of annual surplus, by the co-op's own choice — and treats it as permanent cooperative capital, the accumulated value of the common effort. It is the single strongest structural defence against a later generation of members voting to sell the enterprise and pocket the proceeds.

props.name: Indivisible reserve
props._basis: Canadian Worker Co-op Federation on indivisible reserves; Quebec Cooperatives Act, impartageabilite de la reserve

nodes.label: NET SURPLUS
nodes.note: The residual. It is what is left after the price and the wage have already been set, which is why a co-op can have a fine year with almost no surplus by charging members less and paying members more — and that is not a failure. Judging a hybrid on surplus alone reads the smaller half of this drawing.

nodes.label: NON-MEMBER MARGIN
nodes.note: The share of the surplus earned on business with non-members, plus investment income. It cannot be paid out as patronage to anybody, because no member patronised to create it. It is taxed at corporate rates first, and what survives can only fall into the indivisible reserve — it never reaches a member's hand or a member's account. This is the money argument for recruiting shoppers into membership.

props.name: Non-patronage income
props._basis: IRC Subchapter T; non-member patronage allocated to indivisible reserves on an after-corporate-tax basis

nodes.label: CONSUMER SHARE
nodes.note: Divided among consumer members in proportion to what each one spent. To the member this is a rebate on a purchase, not income, and generally is not taxable to them. Weaver Street moved from an at-the-till discount to an annual dividend in 2009 precisely because a dividend is proportional to actual patronage and a discount is not.

props.name: Consumer patronage allocation
props._basis: Weaver Street Market dividend materials; IRS treatment of a consumer patronage refund as a purchase rebate

nodes.label: WORKER SHARE
nodes.note: Divided among worker members in proportion to hours worked. To the member this is income and fully taxable — including the retained portion they have not yet received in cash, which is the practical reason worker co-ops watch the cash percentage so closely. A dollar sent down this channel is therefore worth less in the member's hand than the same dollar sent down the consumer channel: an asymmetry with no principled justification that nonetheless bears on every split the board sets.

props.name: Worker patronage allocation
props._basis: Weaver Street Market: worker owners pay personal income tax on the entire dividend amount

nodes.label: TAX
nodes.note: A patronage dividend properly allocated is deducted from the co-op's income and taxed once, in the member's hands. Margin that cannot be allocated is taxed here first at corporate rates, and again later if it is ever distributed. The tax code rewards a co-op for being genuinely member-based, and the size of this arrow is the size of that reward foregone.

edges.label: goods
edges.note: Inventory and services bought in. The value arrow points into the co-op and the money arrow for the same trade points back out, drawn as two lines on purpose — they bow apart into the lens shape that is Odum's counterflow.

edges.label: labour
edges.note: The worker member's patronage. This is the arrow that makes them a patron and not merely an employee — it is what the worker share is later allocated in proportion to.

edges.label: goods & service
edges.note: The consumer member's patronage seen from the value side. Its counterflow is the price at the till.

edges.label: the same goods
edges.note: Identical on the value side to what a member gets. The whole difference between a member and a non-member is invisible in the value circuit and shows up only in the money circuit.

edges.label: price at the till
edges.note: COUNTERFLOW to the goods arrow, and price is the ratio of the two at this point. In a co-op the board sets that price, so the first and largest return to consumer members is made right here, silently, and not at the patronage split.

edges.label: same price, no ownership
edges.note: The dollar looks identical arriving. What differs is what the co-op is then allowed to do with the margin on it.

edges.label: cost of goods
edges.note: Counterflow to the goods arrow, and the largest single outflow in a retail hybrid. Add a third producer-member class and this arrow becomes a patronage arrow too, gaining its own column on the right-hand side.

edges.label: WAGES — paid before any surplus exists
edges.note: The counterflow to labour, and the point of the whole drawing. This arrow is an order of magnitude larger than the worker share on the right, and it comes out of the same till as the consumer price. Raise it and either the price rises or the surplus falls. That trade has no technical solution — deciding it is what the board is for.

props.basis: Structural: wages are an operating cost, not a distribution of surplus, under every co-op statute

edges.label: rent, interest, overhead
edges.note: Paid regardless of the year's result, and to people who own no part of the enterprise. Shrinking this arrow is what member capital is for.

edges.label: what is left
edges.note: The residual, and the only part of the money circuit the membership ever votes on directly.

edges.label: set aside first
edges.note: Taken off the top, before either class is allocated anything. Setting this percentage is deciding how much of this year's work belongs to the co-op's future rather than to its present members.

edges.label: by dollars spent
edges.note: The consumer class's share, then divided within the class by each member's purchases.

edges.label: by hours worked
edges.note: The worker class's share, then divided within the class by each member's hours. The class-level split and the within-class split are two different decisions: the first is political, the second is arithmetic.

edges.label: the part earned on non-member business
edges.note: Separated out before anything is allocated, because it is legally a different kind of money.

edges.label: corporate rate — then only the reserve
edges.note: The cost of doing business with people who are not members. What survives the tax cannot be allocated to anyone and joins the indivisible reserve.

edges.label: cash refund — at least 20%, and not taxable to them
edges.note: Subchapter T requires at least 20% of a patronage refund to be paid in money within the statutory period for the co-op to deduct the whole allocation. To the consumer member this is a rebate on purchases and generally is not taxable income.

props.basis: IRC Subchapter T; the 20% cash requirement for a qualified written notice of allocation

edges.label: cash dividend — at least 20%, taxable as income
edges.note: The same 20% rule, a different tax landing. Same rule, same co-op, same year — and the dollar is worth less on arrival.

props.basis: Weaver Street Market: worker owners pay personal income tax on the entire dividend amount

edges.label: retained — up to 80%
edges.note: A qualified written notice of allocation. The member is told the amount, is credited with it, and does not get it yet.

edges.label: retained — up to 80%
edges.note: Mondragon policy caps the cash portion at 30% and sends the bulk to the worker member's internal capital account, where it earns interest until they leave or retire.

props.basis: Mondragon: members receive up to 30% of the distribution in cash, the bulk to an internal capital account

edges.label: share bought at joining
edges.note: One time, and generally small — Lund rates consumer equity contribution LOW. It buys the vote, not the return.

edges.label: stake, by payroll deduction
edges.note: Eroski's worker members buy in over three years by regular deduction; employees of acquired chains get five years and over 95% take it up. Paying in from wages rather than from savings is what makes worker membership reachable for people without capital.

props.basis: Eroski: employees invest their membership through regular deductions over three years

edges.label: this is what finances the business
edges.note: THE LOOP. A co-op's working capital is largely made out of surplus it has already earned and not paid out — not out of investment raised from strangers. Every dollar here is a dollar not borrowed, and it belongs to a named member who will one day take it back.

edges.label: permanent capital — never repaid
edges.note: The difference between this arrow and the one below it is the whole indivisible-reserve argument: this capital has nobody's name on it and no date on which it must be returned.

edges.label: elect the consumer seats
edges.note: One member one vote WITHIN the class. Four thousand consumer owners electing two seats is not four thousand votes against sixty — and that is the design decision the class structure exists to make.

edges.label: elect the worker seats
edges.note: Sixty worker owners electing two seats. Equal board power on radically unequal numbers, justified by the difference in stake rather than the difference in count.

edges.label: sets the split — the half that is put to the members
edges.note: The decision members can see and will argue about at the annual meeting. Lund: a co-op may decide the bulk of the surplus belongs first to those whose livelihood depends on it — usually the workers — or it may not. There is no correct answer and no US federal law supplies one; each hybrid writes it into its own bylaws and pays a lawyer for the privilege.

props.basis: Lund, 'Distribution of Surplus'; there is no overarching US federal co-op law

edges.label: sets PRICE and WAGE — the bigger half, made quietly
edges.note: Same body, same year, same till. This arrow and the one to NET SURPLUS are two halves of one distributive act, and only one half is ever put to a vote. A hybrid that debates its patronage formula while treating price and wage as management detail has hidden its main distributive decision from its own owners.
